name: Barbera

lines.s10: Barbera is Piedmont's everyday red, deep in colour and juicy with sour cherry, its acidity high and its tannin gentle.
lines.s20: Barbera is the red that Piedmont pours every day, from the hills of Asti and Alba. It is dark and juicy, with sour cherry and black plum, mouth watering acidity and very little tannin.
lines.s45: Barbera breaks the rule that a dark red must be a hard one. It is the everyday red of Piedmont, at home in the hills of Asti and Alba. It pours deep purple and tastes of sour cherry and black plum, with mouth watering acidity and very little tannin. Much of it is made simply, while the Barbera of Nizza often spends time in small oak barrels that add vanilla and a firmer frame. California Barbera, from the Sierra Foothills, tends to be riper and fuller, yet just as bright. It loves tomato sauce, salumi and pizza. In Piedmont it is the family's daily bottle, opened while the Barolo waits.
lines.sale: Barbera has the juicy acidity that makes cured meats and a tomato sauce taste brighter, and almost no tannin to fight them. A Barbera d'Asti, served a touch cool, is what I would pour with the pasta or the charcuterie.

glass.lead: Sour cherry and black plum in a deep purple glass, with mouth watering acidity and soft, low tannin.

ladder.where: The hills of Asti, Nizza and Alba, and the Monferrato
The Sierra Foothills and Lodi in California, and McLaren Vale

glass.structure: Dry. Acidity high to very high, tannin low to medium, alcohol medium plus, body medium; deep in colour for so soft a red.

old.where: Piedmont's Asti, Nizza, Alba and Monferrato; Gutturnio in the Piacenza hills
old.glass: Tends to be sharp and juicy: sour cherry, red plum and dried thyme over very high acidity, little tannin and medium body.
old.cellar: Everyday Barbera is often kept in steel or large old casks; Nizza and Superiore spend months in wood, often small French barrels.

new.where: California's Sierra Foothills and Lodi; Australia's McLaren Vale
new.glass: Typically riper and rounder: black cherry, blackberry and plum jam, with higher alcohol and often vanilla from oak, the acidity still bright beneath.
new.cellar: Labelled by the grape and usually aged in oak barrels, a share of them new; much of California's crop once went into blends.

contrast.why: Barbera holds its acidity even in heat, so warm New World sites ripen it to darker fruit and more alcohol while it stays fresh. Piedmont's rules tie it to Asti, Nizza or Alba and their ageing laws.
contrast.blur: A warm year's Nizza or Barbera d'Alba in new French barrels can match California's plush vanilla; the cooler Adelaide Hills and King Valley make fresher, less jammy Barbera.
contrast.call: Sour cherry, dried thyme and a sharp, juicy finish lean Piedmont; jammy black cherry, vanilla and higher alcohol lean California or Australia.

service.temp: 59 to 63 degrees Fahrenheit, 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; a young, unoaked one a little cooler.
service.glass: A Burgundy bowl, or a standard red wine glass for an everyday bottle.
service.decant: Usually unnecessary; a young, barrel aged Nizza may open with air after a taste.
service.age: Three to eight years: everyday Barbera sooner, Nizza and Superiore at the long end.

with.why: the wine's acidity matches the tomato's own
acidity cuts the fat, and low tannin spares the salt
juicy fruit and no hard edges beside tomato and cheese
bright acidity and soft tannin beside the smoky sausage

labels.means: The DOCG of the hills around Asti, at least 90 per cent Barbera; Superiore means longer ageing, partly in wood.
Barbera alone from around Nizza Monferrato, its own DOCG since 2014, aged 18 months, 6 in wood.
The Langhe's Barbera, from the hills around Alba; often plusher and fuller than Barbera d'Asti.
A wine, not a grape: Barbera with Croatina from the Piacenza hills of Emilia.

guest.a: Same hills, different grape. Barolo is Nebbiolo, pale with a fierce grip. Barbera is darker and juicier, soft in tannin and bright in acidity, the bottle Piedmont opens while its Barolo ages.

guest.q: Why does this red make my mouth water?
guest.a: That is Barbera's high acidity. With so little tannin, the freshness is what you feel, and it is why the wine suits tomato sauces and cured meats.

guest.q: Is the California one very different?
guest.a: Usually riper and fuller, with black cherry, more alcohol and more vanilla from oak barrels, but the same bright acidity runs through it.

compare.tell: Dolcetto is the low acid one, soft and round, with a little more tannin and a bitter almond finish; Barbera is sharper, juicier and gentler in grip.
Nebbiolo from the same hills is the opposite: pale garnet with high tannin; Barbera is deep purple, with high acidity and little tannin.
Sangiovese shares the high acidity but adds tomato leaf and a dusty, firmer tannin; Barbera is deeper in colour, juicier and softer in grip.

cards.front: Barbera blind: what upside down structure gives it away?
cards.back: Deep colour with very high acidity and low tannin: the reverse of Nebbiolo, which is pale with high tannin, from the same hills.

cards.front: Barbera, Old World or New World: what does a blind taster lean on?
cards.back: Sour cherry, dried thyme and a sharp, juicy finish lean Piedmont. Jammy black cherry, vanilla and higher alcohol lean California or Australia.

cards.front: Nizza: which grape, since when its own DOCG, and how long aged?
cards.back: Barbera alone. Nizza became its own DOCG in 2014; it ages at least 18 months, 6 of them in wood, and Riserva 30 months with 12.

questions.q: Two glasses of Barbera are poured blind. One shows sour cherry, dried thyme and a sharp, juicy finish; the other jammy black cherry, vanilla and higher alcohol. Which pair of origins fits, in that order?
questions.exp: Sharp sour cherry fruit at moderate ripeness tends to mark Piedmont; riper, jammier fruit, vanilla from oak and more alcohol tend to mark a warm California site. The reversed pair swaps the two.

questions.q: A red poured blind is deep purple, with sour cherry and black plum, very high acidity and almost no tannin. Which Piedmont grape is it?
questions.exp: Deep colour, very high acidity and low tannin is Barbera's signature. Dolcetto, the nearest wrong option, is the low acid grape with firmer tannin, and Nebbiolo is pale with high tannin.

questions.q: A guest wants a Piedmont red for salumi and a tomato pasta: fresh, juicy and with almost no tannin. Which do you pour?
questions.exp: Barbera d'Asti brings the high acidity tomato and cured meat ask for, with little tannin. Dolcetto d'Alba, the nearest miss, is softer in acidity and firmer in tannin; Barolo and Ghemme are Nebbiolo and grip hard.

report: Mode contrast, as the plan fixes it, though TASTE.world is old: the plan's modeWhy sets Piedmont against California, where Barbera has grown since the late nineteenth century. A reviewer may weigh whether a guest truly meets a New World Barbera on a list; the Sierra Foothills, Lodi and the King Valley do bottle it under the grape's name.

Piedmont facts (Barbera d'Asti and Nizza the DOCGs, Barbera d'Alba the plusher Langhe wine, barrique often given to tame its acid, Gutturnio as Barbera with Croatina from the Piacenza hills) stand on the Codex's Piedmont and Emilia-Romagna records. Nizza as 100 per cent Barbera, its own DOCG since 2014, 18 months with 6 in wood and Riserva 30 with 12 stands on the Nizza association's regulation page and trade sources.

Barbera d'Asti at least 90 per cent Barbera stands on trade sources that compare it with Nizza; Superiore as longer ageing partly in wood stands on the Codex's pairing record. The exact Superiore months (14 with 6 in wood, by one producer's page) are left out.

California: the grape kept its high acidity in hot districts and went largely into blends (University of California fact sheet), arrived in the 1880s (Lodi Wine, citing the university) and became a wine bottled by its name in the Sierra Foothills. Australia: arrived with Italian migrants in the King Valley and the Riverina, then McLaren Vale and Mudgee (Wine Selectors). The sites were read through search results only; a checker should open them.

Barbera's GRAPES profile writes the acid as VERY HIGH and TASTE gives tannin 0; the structure line gives acidity high to very high and tannin low to medium, as the profile's own st does. INTRO_GRAPES gives body 2 and TASTE body 1; the line says medium.
The Creole dish is a chicken and andouille gumbo, where the wine's acidity and soft tannin sit with the smoked sausage.
